transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-09
Start time: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Connor Liu (Redwood SE), Oliver Grant (CTO - Stratus Data), Priya Rao (Lead ML Engineer), Samir Khan (Platform Engineer)

Summary:
Quick integration discovery focused on how Stratus Data would integrate Redwood Hosted/Dedicated/Private. Key topics: SDKs and LangChain/LlamaIndex compatibility, gateway/proxy architecture, rate limits and quotas, observability hooks (tracing, token-level cost), and security requirements (SAML, KMS, SOC2). Next steps: Redwood to share integration snippets, pricing, and sample configs for gateway/proxy and observability.

Topics:
- SDK support and example flows (Python, Node)
- LangChain / LlamaIndex adapters and recommended patterns
- Gateway/proxy vs direct SDK calls (auth, egress, caching)
- Rate limiting, quotas, burst handling, and throttling behavior
- Observability hooks: traces, per-model metrics, token cost breakdowns
- Security: SSO/SAML, audit logs, KMS encryption, data residency

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, appreciate ya squeezing us in. Quick intros — I'm Maya, account lead for Redwood, and with me is Connor, our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Oliver: Hi, I'm Oliver, CTO at Stratus Data. Priya and Samir are with me. We mostly run inference for search/rerank and some summarization pipelines.
[00:21] Priya: Hey all. We're trying to figure out whether Hosted makes sense or we need Dedicated or Private for compliance and latency.
[00:30] Connor: Cool, sounds good. Maybe high level — can you share current traffic shape? QPS, 99th percentile latency you're targeting, and any red lines on data leaving your VPC?
[00:41] Samir: Sure, our peak QPS for the search assistant is about 120 req/s now, bursts to ~250 for sales events. Target 99p latency for single-turn generation is sub-250 ms if possible — that's tough — and summaries can be 500–800 ms okay. Data residency: all customer PII must stay in our AWS account or flow through an approved private link.
[01:05] Connor: Got it. That pushes toward Dedicated or Private because of residency + burst needs, but Hosted can still work with VPC egress and private endpoints depending on the plan. Quick note — our Dedicated pools give predictable throughput and you can pin GPU types; Private gives you a customer-managed control plane.
[01:20] Maya: One of the things we're keen to cover today is the integration surface — SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors, and whether you should run a gateway or call the SDK directly from your microservices.
[01:31] Priya: Yeah, we've standardized on LangChain + LlamaIndex for retrieval-augmented generation. We have orchestration via Airflow and a platform layer that expects a simple HTTP gateway to rate limit and add auth context.
[01:43] Connor: Perfect. We provide official SDKs in Python and Node that are drop-in for most patterns. For LangChain, we have an adapter pattern — it's basically a small connector you can plug into the LLM wrapper. It does retries, streaming, and function calling. For LlamaIndex, same idea — you can swap the underlying LLM client to Redwood's SDK with minimal changes.
[02:02] Priya: Any sample code? We need to know how to handle streaming tokens and interruption in our UI.
[02:09] Connor: Yes, I'll send a sample snippet. Example: from redwood import RedwoodClient... then you can stream tokens with on_token callbacks. Note — small caveat in some transcribed docs the example shows 'RedwoodServer' — that's an older name in some places, ignore that.
[02:26] Oliver: Okay, good. About the gateway — do you recommend putting our own proxy in front to handle auth and caching or letting Redwood handle caching at the prefix/KV level?
[02:36] Maya: We see customers do both. Gateway gives you centralized auth, enterprise headers, and local caching for hot prompts. Redwood provides automatic prefix and KV caching and continuous batching which reduces token costs. If you need full control over data egress and extra logic (e.g., rewrite prompts), we often recommend a lightweight gateway + Redwood SDK to the gateway.
[02:54] Samir: If we run a gateway in our VPC, can it talk to Redwood via private link? We can't have tokens leaving over the public internet for certain flows.
[03:02] Connor: Yes, for Dedicated and Private we support VPC peering / PrivateLink options. For Hosted, we have a private endpoint option for enterprise customers — it's effectively a proxy endpoint that terminates in the Redwood infra but only accessible from your VPC.
[03:17] Priya: How does rate limiting and quotas behave? We want per-team quotas and the ability to throttle bursts without dropping requests.
[03:25] Connor: Two layers — client-side and server-side. On the Redwood side we enforce quotas and per-key rate limits; you can set per-route quotas in the Console and apply RBAC for teams. For burst handling, we support token-based throttling and configurable retry-backoff policies. If you're using a gateway, you can enforce soft limits there and buffer or drop based on priority.
[03:44] Oliver: Do you expose headers for remaining quota and retry-after?
[03:48] Connor: Yes, response headers include x-rw-quota-remaining, x-rw-retry-after and per-model latency metrics. We'll provide the full header spec.
[03:56] Priya: Observability — we need traces attached to our request flows and token-level cost breakdowns. Can we get per-request trace ID and instrumentation hooks?
[04:05] Maya: Absolutely. The Console exposes per-route/model dashboards and you can enable tracing. We provide a trace id in the response which you can correlate in your logs; we also have a tracing hook for OpenTelemetry and can ingest spans. Token-level cost breakdowns are available in usage logs and the Console.
[04:21] Samir: On the security side, SOC2 is required. Also we want KMS integration for keys and SAML for SSO. How far along is that?
[04:29] Connor: We're SOC 2 Type II. For keys, we support customer-managed KMS via our Private offering and with Dedicated we can integrate an HSM/KMS for model keys and auditing. SAML SSO is supported with SCIM for provisioning. We'll attach the security pack and SOC2 report after this call.
[04:44] Priya: Great. A couple of technical questions — how do you handle KV cache eviction and multi-tenant isolation? In our profiling, cache hits would be huge for hot queries.
[04:54] Connor: The runtime uses LRU-ish heuristics with adaptive sizing per model; for Dedicated you can reserve cache memory per-tenant to guarantee hit rates. Multi-tenant isolation is enforced at the runtime level — KV entries are namespaced by tenant id and encrypted at rest. There's also eviction policies you can tune.
[05:10] Oliver: About latency — you talked about continuous batching. For our 120–250 QPS bursts, how do you ensure 99p sub-250 ms?
[05:19] Connor: It depends strongly on model and sequence length. We pick kernels and batching windows dynamically; for low-latency SLOs you can pin to a lower-concurrency allocation on Dedicated. We also offer warm pools and pre-warmed KV caches which help tail latency. If you need hard SLOs, Private with local GPUs gives the most predictability.
[05:38] Priya: Any docs on model selection and quantization? We may try a quantized variant to reduce costs but concerned about quality regressions.
[05:46] Maya: Yes, Redwood Optimize provides recommendations — we can run an eval on your top prompts to compare full-precision vs quantized models and give regression alerts. We'll include a sample eval workflow.
[05:58] Samir: If we run a gateway that does batching, is there a risk of double-batching with Redwood's continuous batching?
[06:05] Connor: Good callout. Gateway-side batching should be aware of Redwood's batching behavior; typically you send single logical requests to Redwood and rely on the runtime to batch at token level. If you batch multiple logical requests at the gateway, you may increase latency if your gateway waits to form batches. We can share patterns — usually gateway does only auth, routing, and light caching, while Redwood handles efficient batching.
[06:26] Oliver: About SDKs — how do you handle streaming cancellations and partial responses? Our UI needs to cancel and show partial outputs cleanly.
[06:33] Connor: SDKs expose a cancel handle; when you cancel we send a best-effort cancellation to the runtime and return partial tokens to the client. Note that partial outputs may not be consistent for function-calling flows — we'll document caveats. Also occasional transcriptions we have in old docs use 'redwood-streamer' naming — ignore typos.
[06:54] Priya: Can we run A/B tests with different model variants? We have a canary workflow.
[06:59] Maya: Yep — the Console supports rollout policies and A/B canaries, and you can route by tag, model version, region. We'll show an example canary config.
[07:09] Samir: For logging and retention, our legal team requires 365-day logs and immutable audit trails for admin actions.
[07:16] Connor: We offer extended retention as an add-on for logs and audit trails, plus immutable storage options. For Private deployments you can control retention locally.
[07:27] Priya: Any pitfalls others hit when integrating LangChain?
[07:31] Connor: Common ones — forgetting to handle streaming token order (LangChain's LLM chain sometimes expects final output), not propagating request metadata (user id, tenant id) into prompt engineering, and misconfiguring rate limits so you get throttled. We have an integration guide that highlights these.
[07:48] Oliver: Regarding cost, can you break down token-level cost per model and show how batching affects unit economics?
[07:56] Maya: Yes, Console has token-level cost breakdowns per-model and per-route; Redwood Optimize can suggest batching/caching parameters and show estimated savings. We'll generate a cost model for your traffic once you share sample request distributions.
[08:12] Priya: About model fallbacks — we sometimes want a cheaper model as a fallback if latency or quota issues hit. Does Redwood support automatic fallback?
[08:19] Connor: Smart routing supports policies like fallback to compatible model variants (e.g., a quantized variant) or region-based fallback. You can set automatic fallback triggers on latency or error rates.
[08:30] Maya: Quick clarification — for your compliance constraint, it sounds like a hybrid approach makes sense: Dedicated for the production traffic with a Private control plane in your VPC for sensitive flows, and Hosted for low-risk, internal experiments.
[08:40] Oliver: That was our thought too. One more thing — can you integrate with our existing CI so we can run regression tests on new model versions?
[08:47] Connor: Yep, we have APIs to run evals and webhooks for results. You can plug that into CI to gate rollouts based on LR metrics.
[08:56] Priya: Would you be able to do a short benchmark run against our top 20 prompts? Say, run latency and quality comparisons across three model variants?
[09:04] Maya: Yes, we'll set that up. Connor will own the technical run.
[09:08] Connor: I'll need sample prompts, expected outputs, and a test harness — we'll give you a repo with a harness that uses the SDK or a gateway config.
[09:17] Oliver: Timeline-wise, we want to decide in the next quarter — ideally PoC in 3–4 weeks.
[09:24] Maya: Sounds reasonable. We'll aim to get pricing and SOW first, run the benchmark, then set up a 2–4 week PoC on Dedicated.
[09:31] Samir: Regarding onboarding, how long to turn up a Dedicated pool?
[09:35] Maya: Typical lead time is 1–3 weeks depending on capacity and GPU type. Private on-prem takes longer. We'll note this in the SOW.
[09:42] Priya: For the PoC, we want to test integration with LangChain + our gateway and validate 99p latency and cost.
[09:49] Connor: We'll include a checklist for that PoC.
[09:53] Oliver: Ok, let's recap.
[09:55] Maya: Recap — Redwood to send: 1) Hosted vs Dedicated pricing and example SLOs/SOW (Maya) 2) LangChain/LlamaIndex integration guide + SDK snippets + sample gateway config (Connor) 3) Security pack and SOC2 report (Connor/Maya) 4) Redwood to run benchmark on top prompts once provided (Connor). Stratus to send top prompts, histograms, and decision timeline (Oliver/Priya).
[10:20] Priya: Sounds good. Anything else?
[10:23] Samir: No, thanks.
[10:25] Maya: Great — we'll follow up with notes and the repo links. Thanks all.

End of transcript.
